senses.d: A large, highly organized military force, concerned mainly with ground (rather than air or naval) operations.
ex: An army never can be commanded or controlled by civilians.
The army was sent in to quell the uprising.

senses.d: Used absolutely for that entire branch of the armed forces.
ex: The army received a bigger share of this year's budget increase than the navy or air force.

senses.d: Within a vast military, a very large tactical contingent (e.g. a number of divisions).
ex: The Fourth Army suffered such losses that its remainders were merged into the Second Army, also deployed on the Western front.

senses.d: The governmental agency in charge of a state's army.
ex: The army opposed the legislature's involvement.

senses.d: A large group of people working toward the same purpose.
ex: It took an army of accountants to uncover the fraud.
On sunny days the beaches draw armies of tourists of all kinds.

senses.d: A large group of animals, especially caterpillars or social insects working toward the same purpose.
ex: Our house is being attacked by an army of ants.

senses.d: Any multitude.
ex: There was an army of construction cranes working on building the skyscraper.

senses.d: The military as a whole.
ex: The People's Liberation Army Navy of China.
The Yugoslav Army consisted of the War Navy, Ground Forces, and Air Force.

ety.text: From Middle English arm, from Old English earm (Anglian arm), from Proto-West Germanic *arm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz (“arm”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“a fitting, joint; arm, forequarter”), a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to join, fit together”). Cognates Akin to Dutch arm, German Arm, Yiddish אָרעם (orem), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish arm.

From Middle English arm (“poor, wretched”), from Old English earm (“poor, miserable, pitiful, wretched”), from Proto-West Germanic *arm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz (“poor”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erm- (“poor, ill”). Cognates Akin to Dutch arm (“poor”), German arm (“poor”), Yiddish אָרעם (orem, “poor”), Swedish arm (“poor”).

Back-formation from arms (plural), from Middle English armes, from Old French armes, from Latin arma (“weapons”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-mo-, a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to fit together”), hence ultimately cognate with etymology 1.

senses.d: The extended portion of the upper limb, from the shoulder to the elbow.

ex: the arms of an octopus

ex: The robot arm reached out and placed the part on the assembly line.
